gloss: To put a seed or a young plant into the ground so that it will grow.
examples: We *plant* tomatoes every year around Mother's Day.

gloss: To prepare and use land for growing crops, or to grow a particular crop.

His family *cultivated* the same hillside for a hundred years.

gloss: To break up and turn over soil so that it is ready for planting.

He *tilled* four acres before breakfast.
The field has been *tilled* and is ready for seed.

transitivity: both — transitive (plow the north field), intransitive (they plowed until dark)

The ground has already been *plowed* twice.

gloss: To scatter seed over a piece of ground.

They *seeded* the pasture with clover.
The burned slope is being *seeded* by hand.

gloss: To dig up a plant and plant it somewhere else.

She *transplanted* the roses to a sunnier bed.
The little oak has been *transplanted* twice already.

gloss: To plant something again, or to plant new plants where old ones were.

They *replanted* the whole hillside after the fire.

gloss: To add something to soil or plants to make them grow better.

He *fertilized* the lawn in April.
The rows have been *fertilized* and watered.
contrast: American spelling ends in -ize: fertilize, fertilized. British English writes fertilise.

gloss: To cover soil with bark, straw, or leaves to hold in water and stop weeds.

transitivity: both — transitive (weed the garden), intransitive (she weeded all morning)

transitivity: both — transitive (hoe the bean rows), intransitive (he hoed until noon)

transitivity: both — transitive (rake the leaves), intransitive (we raked all afternoon)

He *raked* the gravel smooth.

gloss: To move dirt, snow, or manure with a shovel.

gloss: To cut branches off a tree or bush so it grows better.

transitivity: both — transitive (the pines shelter the barn), intransitive (the cattle sheltered under the trees)

They *dammed* the stream to make a stock pond.
The river has been *dammed* since 1940.
contrast: Doubles the m: dam → dammed, damming — which then looks like damn, a different word entirely.

ru: отводить, отвести (воду); направлять в другую сторону
gloss: To make water or traffic go a different way.
examples: Growers *divert* river water into the orchards.
They *diverted* the creek around the new field.
The stream has been *diverted* twice in ten years.

transitivity: both — intransitive (the ducks splash), transitive (the calf splashed us with mud)
gloss: To move through water noisily, or to throw water around.
examples: The ducks *splash* in the trough all day.
The calf *splashed* straight through the mud.
The kids were *splashing* around in the creek.
contrast: Third person takes -es after -sh: it splashes.

gloss: To fill a place in large harmful numbers, said of insects or pests.
examples: Beetles *infest* the corn every August.
Aphids *infested* the whole greenhouse in a week.
The old barn is *infested* with mice.
contrast: Usually passive: the field is infested with weevils — the preposition is with.

gloss: To put a person, animal, or species at risk of harm or of dying out.
examples: Logging *endangers* dozens of bird species.
The drought *endangered* the whole herd.
Sea turtles are *endangered* almost everywhere.

gloss: To hide something by making it look like what is around it.
examples: Brown feathers *camouflage* the hen on her nest.
The moth *camouflaged* itself against the bark.
The nest was *camouflaged* with moss and grass.
contrast: Spelling trap: -mou- in the middle and -flage at the end, but it ends in the sound -flahzh.

transitivity: both — transitive (farm four hundred acres), intransitive (they farm for a living)
gloss: To use land to grow crops or raise animals.
examples: They *farm* four hundred acres of wheat.
His family *farmed* this land for sixty years.
The valley has been *farmed* since the 1800s.

gloss: To work in a garden growing flowers or vegetables.
examples: My parents *garden* every weekend from April on.
She *gardened* well into her eighties.
He has been *gardening* since the snow melted.

gloss: To cut down a tree.
examples: The crew *fells* the dead pines first.
They *felled* the old oak in under an hour.
Thousands of trees have been *felled* on this slope.
contrast: Not the same as fell, the past of fall. The tree fell on its own; the crew felled the tree.

transitivity: both — intransitive (the cattle stampeded), transitive (the thunder stampeded the herd)
gloss: To run in a sudden panic, said of a herd of animals.
examples: Cattle *stampede* at the first crack of thunder.
The herd *stampeded* straight through the fence.
The horses were *stampeding* toward the river.

gloss: To burn a mark into an animal's hide to show who owns it.
examples: Ranchers *brand* the calves every spring.
They *branded* two hundred head that weekend.
Every steer here is *branded* on the left hip.

transitivity: both — transitive (the calf nuzzled its mother), intransitive (the horse nuzzled at my hand)
gloss: To push or rub gently with the nose or mouth.
examples: The foals *nuzzle* your pockets looking for treats.
The calf *nuzzled* its mother and started to feed.
The horse was *nuzzling* my shoulder the whole time.

transitivity: both — transitive (the horse pawed the ground), intransitive (the dog pawed at the door)
gloss: To scrape or touch something with a foot or hoof.
examples: Horses *paw* the ground when they get impatient.
The dog *pawed* at the barn door until we opened it.
A mare was *pawing* through the snow for grass.
contrast: Paw at something when the animal keeps touching it: the cat paws at the window.

gloss: To roll around in mud or water, said of animals.
examples: Hogs *wallow* in the mud to stay cool.
The buffalo *wallowed* in a dust hole all afternoon.
Two pigs were *wallowing* by the fence.

gloss: To move in small waves across a surface.
examples: The wheat *ripples* whenever the wind crosses the field.
The pond *rippled* where a fish came up.
The tall grass was *rippling* like water.

gloss: To improve a piece of ground by planting and shaping it.
examples: They *landscape* yards for a living.
We *landscaped* the slope with native grasses.
The whole property has been *landscaped*.

gloss: To pull out some young plants so the rest have room to grow.
examples: *Thin* the carrots once they are two inches tall.
We *thinned* the apples so the rest would grow bigger.
The lettuce has been *thinned* twice already.
contrast: Doubles the n: thin → thinned, thinning.
